utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Let's start, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. May I first introduce a new member of our team, our Defence team here in the courtroom, he's Mr. Enrico Boninsega, my legal assistant, and I would like to welcome him to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the motion you -- regarding your question as for the remuneration of Mr. Donia, having reconsidered the substance, the Chamber is of the opinion, given the position of the Prosecution and given the fact that you may have access through other channels, we allow the question, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll come to that if need be, and I think it will be important, yes. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, Mr. Donia. For you and I to go home as quickly as possible, I have prepared a set of facts about which we could reach an agreement, I believe, and for us to do that, I'd like the document to be distributed to everybody in the courtroom, and I'd expect you, kindly expect you, to -- and request you to take a look at the document and to confirm the facts that you know took place. These are, generally speaking, court decisions on various events. Now, I don't expect you to speak to the legal side of the question but just to tell us whether these events happened, and thus we could reduce the facts that we have to contest -- or, rather, which we have to prove through you. So just the historical aspects from you, please, in view of the fact that you dealt with this crisis. Just tell us whether those things actually took place. We have a version in Serbian and another one in English. You can do that tomorrow or whenever you have time, if you agree and if all the participants agree. That could shorten our time, because then I wouldn't have to present proof and evidence about these events if you say they're well known to you and did happen. This part of agreed facts only refer to the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, and this is important for us not to have to go back to history -- or, rather, the history of the crisis itself. So if the Trial Chamber agrees and the Prosecution agrees, then we can hear your views on that document over the next few days and then that would be placed ad acta. We would have finished with that, and we wouldn't have to wonder whether -- well, we don't have to say whether the constitutional court made a lawful decision or not just whether it took that decision or not. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, just looking through this at first glance, it appears to me to deal exclusively with legal decisions of courts and perhaps Assemblies. I certainly -- I'm familiar with a few of these but would not want to attest to the complete accuracy probably of the vast majority of them simply because I would need to view the actual decisions as a document. I think again, just quickly passing through this, it looks to me like a lot of this is knowable from documentation but not from my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on. But speaking for myself, I think the Prosecution may be able to answer these questions on its own, apart from the fact that Dr. Donia may be able to confirm or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In any case, just having received the document, Your Honours, we'll be able to give you an answer in due course if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Whether the Prosecution or the witness, it would be useful if you could confirm these facts so that we can finish with them. I'm not going into the legal aspects of it, just whether a court took a particular decision or Assembly. It doesn't matter what kind and whether it was lawful to do so or not, but just to reduce the scope of the facts that we have to deal with and perhaps challenge, which are not contentious at all. Thank you. May we continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you'll remember that there were these two attempts to adopt the declaration on sovereignty in the spring of 1991, and at the same time meetings began with the presidents of the republics or Presidencies of the republics, Yugoslav republics, with respect to resolving the crisis; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware of one attempt to have the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopt the sovereignty declaration, but there certainly was one, and that was indeed followed by the meetings of the -- the round-robin meetings of the six presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have on e-court 1D37, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that the secretary of the Assembly, Avdo Campara, confirmed that 20 deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party had the right to send this document to the council for national equality for review, and that was the basis for putting off the whole thing, the adoption. Postponing it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is -- what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right? Did you confirm that, that Campara gave an interpretation of why a postponement was necessary or why it should be forwarded to the Council for National Equality. And that was on the 27th of February, I believe, 1991, early spring.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he provided a ruling that any 20 deputies of the Assembly on appealing the matter at hand would cause the proposal to be referred to the Council on National Equality, which did not exist, and therefore that there could not be a vote on the measure. It could be discussed but could not be voted upon until such time as the Council of National Equality had ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you speak our language. Can you see in that highlighted portion, and we have the translation as well, that where Izetbegovic in Split, after one of these meetings says the following: That the declaration on sovereignty has already been submitted to the BH Assembly and will most probably be adopted. If it is not adopted with the agreement of the SDS, it will be adopted without it. So from Split he is sending us this message that we're not important. And lower down we have the position of President Milosevic set out in response to the question. This is a press conference held in Split. He says: "Peaceful resolution of the problems is possible in a democratic manner. The fate of Yugoslavia can only be decided only by its own peoples," et cetera, et cetera. So do you agree that Izetbegovic set out this message from Split that he would adopt this regardless of what the Serbs thought?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite in the way that you formulated it. I believe that he referred to the agreement of the SDS, not -- not to Serbs. And, in fact, was clearly stating a position at the beginning of these negotiations or in the course of these negotiations amongst the six presidents of the republics, which indeed eventually ended in a -- an agreement endorsed by all six presidents in Sarajevo on June 6. I believe you were there but not a direct participant. And reaffirmed again on June 12th. So I don't take this as an absolute statement that this is never going to happen. I take it as a, perhaps, one volley in the course of the negotiating process that was just really beginning at this time. By the way, can I ask this is Politika; is that correct? I see, okay. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Politika of the 30 of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very familiar type set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May this document be admitted. And in the meantime, Mr. Donia, let me say that my point is that it's going to be adopted even without the agreement of the SDS and the SDS represented 90 per cent of the Serb people and had the support of all the other Serbs from the other parties in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not have the support of all the other Serbs from the other parties. Had the support of some, and in fact the whole the proposition was strongly opposed by some Serbs who were in other parties at the time and later. I understand your point, and he clearly says that here referencing the SDS, not the Serbs but the SDS. I would, however, say that I think it is a statement of general approach to the negotiations and not a definitive absolute commitment to make this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, with respect, yes, Your Honour, because this is an incomplete, half-page extract from a further collection of extracts of a newspaper article the source of which Dr. Donia actually was able to guess at because he recognised the typeset, of which only two very small portions have been identified for translation. And if this is going to be considered, I would suggest we have the article, at least, as a whole before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the quoted part is too short, so pursuant -- we accept Ms. Edgerton's observation, so we'll admit the entirely article, and so while it is to be translated and tendered, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, this is the paper's identification. I have page 1. But whenever we tender into evidence a portion of an article, we have nothing against having the whole article admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, this was the 30th of March, and the press -- it was a press conference of all six presidents in Split, and this is Izetbegovic's statement. Now, did it actually happen later on that the declarations was indeed adopted on the 15th of October without the agreement of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a different declaration, and it had a very different text than the one that was taken out of consideration on the 27th of February. Having said that, what is normally referred to as a declaration of sovereignty, along with a platform of the Presidency, were both adopted without the participation and over the objections of the SDS on October 15, in the very early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that on the 31st of March, and the very next day -- or, rather, the very next day, a special unit of the MUP intervened at lake Plitvice, the Plitvice lakes, and that there was an armed conflict between the Specials of the MUP of Croatia and members of the militia or police of Knin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear, we're -- Plitvice's in Croatia, so we're not talking about anything that happened in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But not that far off. They did affect us. Plitvice aren't that far off from us.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely certain of that date. I believe that's about right. There was indeed an armed conflict between the -- I thought it was the JNA that was also involved, but in any case, between the police of the Republic of Croatia and a local paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it was the regular police force, not local paramilitary units. There was a clash between the MUP of Croatia at Plitvice and the ordinary local police, and they were opposed to the disarmament and taking away the reserve weapons from the area. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how was it then in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just gave you my understanding of it, and would I actually have to reference documentation to be confident of my memory of it, but to my recollection, the regular police force of Croatia came into conflict with a Serbian paramilitary unit, and there was a substantial conflict in Plitvice, at the -- at the park.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that also on the 31st of March the Patriotic League was founded, which the Party of Democratic Action established as its military wing? And let me just remind you and tell you what Dzevad Pasic says about that in his book "Bosnia and Tuzla, between east and west," on page 223: "The military wing, the first military wing within the frameworks of the SDA was established by the Municipal Board of this party in Sarajevo on the 31st of March, 1991. The idea to form a military organisation came from Alija Izetbegovic, and in Sarajevo it was accepted straight away and put into practice." Does that agree with your findings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see the document that you're citing as evidence for that, and if I could see the context in which this statement is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is in the book, but it's your subject matter, and on the basis of that subject you wrote a number of books and a number of articles; right? Precisely on that same subject matter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you put to me an assertion which actually had several different provisions, and I am prepared to accept some of them, but I would like to see on what -- what source you have -- you are citing to present this as an authoritative disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, for the time being let me ask you this: Do you agree that on the 31st of March, that is a day after the conference in Split, the Patriotic League was formed as the military wing of the Democratic Action Party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now have called up on e-court 1D01393, please. And let me tell you that we're dealing with the 12th of February. I'm sure there is a translation of this document because it has an OTP number -- or, rather, an EDS number. It's a letter which I sent to all the Municipal Boards of the Serb Democratic Party, to the local boards and to all the activists, informing them that it was noticed that flats were being marked and identified if they belonged to military officers, first and foremost, and that rumours were going round about the distribution of weapons. So I'm going to read this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There may not be a need for Dr. Karadzic to read, because this is, I'm informed, 65 ter number 01458, and translation of that document is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bring up the translation of this. 01458. I think we now have it before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, could you please have a look at this document. Let me tell you what this is about. Obviously on the basis of this document we have two concerns. One is the marking of Serb apartments and apartments belonging to military officers, and the second one is the fact that weapons are being distributed. So I recommend to our members to report things like that if they happen, that they continue marking everything so that they would not be able to tell what it was that they had marked and what they had not marked. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware -- I'm aware of the document. I've -- I've seen the document before. The practices I don't know anything about in that period. I really couldn't say that it was happening or not happening. I think the -- the document itself speaks to an effort to bring the Municipal Boards of the SDS into alignment and to, let's say, heighten their vigilance and to make sure that any incidents that they may observe should be reported both to the party and to the local police station and to the -- I guess to the JNA. If one says "nearest garrison," that can only refer to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this is quite in line with what was known about Martin Spegelj's activities, regardless of whether it was actually happening or not, isn't it a fact that uncertainty was growing at the time and that this is highly reminiscent of what Martin Spegelj said, "Ring the doorbell, shoot them in the stomach"; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So why is there this anxiety and concern? Are you saying it has nothing to do with the disclosure of what Spegelj said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my answer last week one time, I don't see that at this time the concern of regarding Mr. Spegelj's -- the video-tape and his statements had much echo in Bosnia at that time. It certainly didn't seem to affect you very much. You were, at this time, in a coalition. In fact, you had just entered into a coalition government with the HDZ and the SDA. I'd even say the language of this memo that you just showed me is one that is hardly alarmist. It is simply a cautionary warning to collect information if you see certain things taking place. So I think that the -- I think there's a lot of ways in which the situation in Croatia did eventually translate into tensions in Bosnia, but I think that at this point to draw a direct line between the Spegelj video and concern about these activities is probably not one that -- that most Bosnians did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you agree that at that point in time Yugoslavia was still in existence and that the Serb people in Croatia and the Serb people in Bosnia and the Serb people in Serbia are the same people, one and the same people, and that the Croatian people in Croatia, the Croatian people in Bosnia, and the Croatian people in Serbia are one and the same people as well? So why do you think that this kind of drastic thing like the uncovering of subversive activity on the part of the minister of defence of Croatia would not affect all of Yugoslavia, particularly army personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you believe that this had no influence whatsoever and that this did not cause concern or anxiety among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- there are three questions I see that you've put to me, and as I -- relative to the first one, as I have indicated, I think that the notion of a single Serb people is a convenient abstraction that, in fact, glosses over differences among and between Serbs and that it is a notion that came to be an obsession with nationalist Serb politicians, including yourself, in the period of 1991 and early 1992. Your -- your other questions presuppose that I accept your -- your notion of a single Serb people, and I just don't -- don't share that, and furthermore, don't agree that this Spegelj tape had anywhere near the impact among the average JNA soldiers and on the streets or in the cafes of Bosnia-Herzegovina as you suggest. It was a well-publicised event that certainly grabbed headlines for a few days. It, in a sense, gave notice to people that the Republic of Croatia was in the business of gathering arms, but it also indicated, as I say, the far-reaching sweep of KOS, the counter-intelligence service of the JNA, and I don't know that it had much of an impact on the level of concern or anxiety among Serbs in Bosnia in general at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this document is proof for you that there was anxiety, but, Mr. Donia, yet again we have to go back to professor Paula Pickering. And you supported her assimilationist views, that new nations could be created, et cetera. Would you recommend to the Jew that is they become Palestinians because they're living in Palestine?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure Professor Pickering will be shocked to hear you characterise her views as assimilationist. They're actually quite -- quite the opposite. I think that the question is -- derives from just a totally false understanding of what I have incorporated in my paper in terms of identity being constructed and -- and flexible over time and that it really doesn't have anything to do with assimilation or any kind of massive shift of identity or capitulation. It talks about how nationalities are formed, how they are maintained, how their foundations may shift over time, but it's not a moral judgement or any kind of imperative for any sort of change in identity that doesn't come about through the processes indigenous to the nationality itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Donia, let's try to distinguish between some things now. One thing that we always have to do as far as your views are concerned, is this a scholar or scientific point of view or political view; namely the Serbs in Serbia and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina are not one and the same people? Is that your political position or is this your position as a scholar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is my position exactly as you've stated it. I have cited the rather voluminous scholarly literature which now comes down strongly on the side of the view that nations are constructed entities and they are imagined by those who make them up or claim loyalty to them. That's a -- they say what I would call close to a consensus view amongst the scholarship now. It is expressly not political in character, but it is used, that viewpoint or those related viewpoints, are used to investigate the sources of identity and the development of identity and behaviour of peoples. And I have, as I say, been influenced by it in making the inquiry that I have made here. So is it -- is it a scholarly, let's say work? Yes, it is a scholarly work, I believe. It is not derived from political but, rather, from, let's say, scholarly -- I benefitted greatly from the insights and conclusions of other scholars in pursuing it and would find that this is, in fact, a superior methodology or approach to employ in understanding those things. I actually thought you kind of liked this because it goes to your own quest for understanding about the relationship between folk, literature folk, poetry, and group psychology. And I think this is an interesting window into that world which is, I'm sure, different from your own but, in fact, related to the things that interest you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you are I are not going to be going home very soon if we go into all of this. My question was whether the democratic right of the Serbs of Croatia and Serbs in Bosnia and Serbs in Serbia is to consider themselves one and the same people, especially after 1918 and they started living together, united in the same state. Is that not their democratic right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they collectively formulate and assert that right, I think -- I think it is. I think the more important, let's say, principle of democracy is that people and not nations get to vote and choose, and to break them down exclusively into national entities which deny the overall right of citizens to vote is, to me, a negation of democratic principles, not an affirmation of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where does that exist in the world? Does that exist in northern Ireland? Does that exist in Spain? Does that exist in the Near East, or the Middle East? Where does that exist where the people can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are we heading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, agree with you. We've gone into an academic discussion. I'm just asking Mr. Donia to tell me on the basis of what one can believe that the Serbs of the former Yugoslavia are different peoples. If Mr. Donia believes that that's possible, then is it not their democratic right to consider themselves one and the same people, even more so because Mr. Donia believes that Muslims in Serbia are Bosniaks although they had never lived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, tell me, do you believe that what happened to Serbs in Croatia did not affect the Serbs of Bosnia, taking into account -- or not taking into account the fact that Bosnia was a part of the Independent State of Croatia during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a number of questions you've raised here and I'm not too sure where -- where to go first. I don't -- I consider the identity of any people to be what they proclaim it to be, recognising that there are always differences and distinctions within that group which make them, in some cases, separate subgroups or in other cases, in fact, groups that split off from what might be called the nation or people as a whole. What I am rejecting is the notion that this is a monolithic homogenous clearly bounded whole that has an entity, that has no distinctions within it and can be represented by one voice, one party, or one individual. That's what I'm rejecting. And I continue to reject that notion. I know that's a notion you live by. You made it the centre of your creed dating back to the programme or speech that you made to the founding Assembly of the SDS. It is a -- as an assumption, I do not share it. I recognise that it animated a great deal of what you did and in the way that you conceive of it today, but I would point out that it is something that was absolutised in your thinking as something that was incontrovertible, self-evident and indisputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're trying to say. I am asking you whether the things that happened to Serbs in Croatia had any affect on the minds of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the things that happened in Croatia had an impact on all Bosnians. Very little at first, more and more as time went along. And that includes the Serbs of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, did this have an equal impact on all Bosniaks -- Bosnians, Serbs, Croats and Muslims alike? Now that you've expanded the topic, could you tell us whether you think there was any difference in degree, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it probably impacted all of them. Most members of each group perceived these events in Croatia differently and developed, I think, let's say different orientations to them. If you will, they had different favourites. But a lot of people who were without these strong nationalist convictions perceived them simply with dismay as the conflict developed and made more likely that this would spill into -- into Bosnia in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was it that you established that, Mr. Donia? How was it that you established that, that there were a lot of people without nationalist feelings or convictions or whatever you had said? Convictions, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's the essence of the response of the -- those people who considered themselves Yugoslavs or many of those who saw themselves as, first and foremost, opposed to a national division in Bosnia, and they had -- they had press outlets. They had -- they wrote op ed pieces. Probably represented the major press organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina right up until, let's say, the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Professor, the political parties that advocate such views, how many votes did they get, and on the other hand, how many votes did the parties that advocated the preservation of national entities get? Why would media be more important than elections? And we saw that in the elections the three national parties won a lot more than a two-third majority. Wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any of the parties that were elected to offices in 1990 advocated the preservation of national entities. They may have come to embrace that position, but I don't think that they -- I don't think that the voters in 1990 voted for national division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us be very specific. The national parties in Croatia -- I mean, who won the elections in Croatia? Was it some kind of a leftist party or a civic party, or was it the HDZ, President Tudjman's party that won the election? And do you think that it wasn't a national party that won these elections on a national platform rather than on a civic platform? Please let us have shorter answers. Was it a national party that won in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the HDZ won a -- did not win a majority of votes in the election in Croatia. It won the majority of seats in the Assembly, and it won control -- won the office the Presidency, but it did not win the majority of votes. So it was clearly a national party that prevailed in terms of the Assembly seats, but that was not the prevailing voter preference in terms of the actual ballots cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But that was only to be expected. It was quite lawful, as it were. What about Bosnia-Herzegovina? It wasn't the Reformists, the Communists and other such parties that won the elections. It was the national parties, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 1D01379.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Donia, let me tell you what all of this was like. Something was happening in Croatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina you, yourself, said that the three ethnic communities were experiencing this in different ways. Now you're going to see what the Party of Democratic Action was doing. You can read our language. So it's the Party of Democratic Action that is sending its own candidates to this very same Croatia where Serbs and officers of the Yugoslav People's Army are experiencing what they are experiencing. They are being killed. They're being laid off because of their ethnic origins. Now, this political party is sending through the MUP its own members to the MUP of Croatia for training. This is what is written here: "Please find attached a copy of the instructions on the way in which candidates for policeman training -- trainee policemen should be received in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, and you should familiarise your candidates with this. "We would like to note that it is the duty of each and every candidate to take along the referral of the party that we are hereby attaching as well as a birth certificate, marriage certificate," and so on and so forth. Hasan Cengic. Is this not what he is sending?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I should have rose a couple of seconds later but we've just been able to locate a translation of that document. It's not been uploaded in e-court because we just found it but perhaps we could do a couple of things, Your Honour. It would take some time to have it uploaded but we could put it on the ELMO to display it for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm concerned a bit why this is happening so often. Why is the Defence team not able to locate the proper translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, just look at how many people the OTP has, for every person they have a separate team, whereas I have only a few people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's beside the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have been in some discussions with Mr. Robinson with this. We have suggested some modalities for -- that we understand are the appropriate and most effective ways of identify existing translations. I understood that the Defence team was going to pursue those a bit more aggressively. I don't know what happened with that. It may be that they did so and found some bureaucratic obstacles that we weren't aware of, but we've indicated our willingness to assist in any reasonable way in ensuring that they access existing translations at the earliest opportunity for everyone's benefit. We can continue in those discussions. I don't know the status of that. As I say, there are ways of doing so. There may be ways of enhancing those mechanisms and we're happy to discuss with the Defence our knowledge about those mechanisms and any measures that may be taken to make them more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I encourage the continuation of such endeavour. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. In the meantime, we'll take a break at half past 10.00 and we will take a break of 25 minutes, and after which it will go until half past 12.00, at which time we will adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, let me ask you: Do you know the Party of Democratic Action took over the control of MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state organ and that it sent its young men for training in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's false. The first part of your question is false. The -- I'm not quite certain what to -- what to make of this. It was common practice for the Ministries of the Interior of the various republics to exchange cadets for training in other republics. Bosnian police went to Serbia for training and even sometimes for duty. There were Bosnian police involved in -- in police duty in Serbia in the late 1980s, and -- so I don't think this is an extraordinary event. What is unusual about it is that it is under the auspices of the SDA, and why that would be I'm not quite certain, whether they are simply endorsing an existing practice or, in fact, conducting some sort of effort to improve co-operation between the MUPs of the various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we just move the document down. Although you were able to see that it's acting SDA secretary Hasan Cengic. But let's -- let me ask you this: Can the party deal with police matters, matters of cadre and inter-republican co-operation to which it sends only Muslims? Is that party business or is that ministry business?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the -- all parties were seeking to become more engaged in such business starting from, let's say, the spring of 1991. I don't see a list of these people so don't know what their ethnicity or affiliations would be. There was, of course, in -- in the MUP at this time an effort by the minister of the interior and the deputy minister of the interior and to co-operate on creating a unified, effective MUP for Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this may have been part of that effort. It -- that agreement clearly rested upon the two parties, that is the two parties concerned, the SDA and the SDS, supporting, at some level anyway, the cooperative venture. My own impression is that they had some success at this in July and August of 1991, but they increasingly came into opposition from both the SDS and the SDA thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please give me shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But any way, I'd like to tender this document signed by Hasan Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D260.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D01378, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that these are all Muslims? Have a look at the whole list, and you'll see that they're all Muslims. They've arrived in Zagreb, and they're all Muslims. And there are 48 of them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the -- what's -- I can't see the date of the document or the nature of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 20th of June, 1991, and it's a list attached to this other document of Hasan Cengic's. They're already in Zagreb, and they're going back home after a short course. The 20th of June, 1991. Do you know at that time at Vraca there was a school set up by the Ministry of the Interior and that it held courses and regular four-year training and education courses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the school that was used by -- or was the MUP school for training officers and lasted, as you say, some long time. This is clearly a three-day instructional course in Zagreb. I would concur that the first names here, that is the second name on each list, suggests that, at least those I can see are -- are Muslim names. It doesn't necessarily mean that they all declared themselves Muslims in the census or identified themselves as Muslims at the time. And of course it also gives their place of residence. But is not this document prior to the date of the document that you showed me before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here they're going back home for three days, from the 21st to the 24th. They're being given leave to go home, have a brief holiday. But this is some group 1, course 6, and there's not a single Serb there. I don't think there's a single Croat either. The Serbs didn't know about this, nor did they need to go to Croatia, because the school at Vraca does have a school and courses as well. Now, did you know that policemen from Bosnia were going for some kind of education to Croatia when Croatia was already at war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to link this document to the prior document. The prior document was dated as 11th of July, while this is dated sometime in June, 20th of June. Since Dr. Donia raised it, you have to clarify first and then continue with your question. Was that the point, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the first sentence: "Attached we send a copy of the instructions about the way in which the candidates policemen were admit." So this isn't the beginning of that association. It's a continuation of co-operation. And all we see here is them being told what they're going to take and where but that was the practice from the spring of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to be very precise in presenting your questions. At the beginning of your question you said this is attached to the prior document. I'm afraid it is not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously not with that specific one, but it is a fact that it was within the same phenomenon, the same practice of sending Muslims secretly to Croatia for training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your questions without making a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you take a look and tell us where these people are from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're from a number of municipalities. Some in - let's see - Doboj, would be in, sort of, north Central Bosnia. Same with Gracanica. Velika Kladusa and Sasine are in the extreme north-west Bosnia. Tuzla, north-eastern Bosnia. Kladanj, north Eastern Bosnia. Zavidovici, north-eastern Bosnia. A number of places, it is seems to me. Bosanska Krupa, which is a municipality along the border with Croatia. Brcko, right along the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the SDA through the MUP was sending its members to be educated in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I find it unsurprising that it was -- that Bosnia was sending people to Croatia for training, although I don't think it was sending people for their initial several months or several years training at this time, but the fact that they -- the MUP of Bosnia was sending people to Croatia is, to me, unremarkable, part of a broader pattern, but I did not know that -- that that was something that was being done with either the endorsement or participation of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D261, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D01398 next, please. And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Donia, let me ask you this: Do you know that disagreements cropped up straight away in the government because of the abuse -- abuses in the MUP or abuses of the MUP? And you saw the agreement, the partner agreement on the division of power and authority. Do you know that the SDA did not respect that and that the Serbs were not appointed to posts that belonged to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's see. This is -- I take it you're putting a document to me here, and this is an SDS document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very kind. Thank you. 06625.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Donia, do you agree that Mr. Izetbegovic was the president of the council for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that that was the position he occupied? It's what the president of the Presidency or president of the republic has as an office together -- while he's president, the president of this council.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying -- I'm not quite clear that your asserting, that he as president of the Presidency was -- one of his duties was to be the head of the council for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. Do you know that, about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific name of that body, but something that had responsibility for such matters was indeed headed by the Presidency. By the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that Professor Plavsic was the president of the council for the protection of the constitutional order in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see here that on the 25th of July we sent a letter in which we say: "Personnel appointments and dismissals in the MUP, Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly those in the State Security Council have not been carried out according to the inter-party agreement nor according to the constitutional obligation concerning the proportional representation of peoples and state organs. "We kindly ask you to urgently take the necessary measures within your power to address this problem that has arisen." So do you know that we had constant clashes with the SDA because it sabotaged the appointment of cadres who were Serbs to the posts that Serbs were supposed occupy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that you had constant clashes with the SDA on the question of appointments, particularly in the police. And a lot of those agreements or disagreements grew out of the dispute over the nature of the inter-party agreements. While the inter-party agreements specified several specific positions that were to be taken by one -- the appointee of one party or another, it wasn't clear in those agreements how deep into the structure the national composition was to be imposed. And in a lot of cases the police forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a large number of Serbs serving in them. So the disagreements came not only about new appointments to the senior positions in the police forces but also the overall composition of those police forces, and each party, to my understanding, in this period was trying to achieve an ethnic balance, and I think this is what's expressed here, the -- an ethnic balance that corresponded to the composition of the particular municipality or area under -- that was concerned. So a lot of disagreements floated around that issue and amounted to an essentially deep intrusion into the professional ranks of the police as they then became ethnosized since the only way to keep a job, if you were a cop, was basically to seek the protection of the national party concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that, Mr. Donia, but I have put it to you or put it to you a few days ago that the SDS did not bring anybody new to the police and that the highest ranking police officers were not party members, and you more or less confirmed that. However, what I'm talking about here now are the tricks that were played and not legitimate concern. This was a trick, and we're going to prove that when we come to discussion 1991 and other aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the meantime, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D262, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D38, please, since we're dealing with this same month just a day later, the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you what it's about. It's the Serbian Democratic Party document or the Municipal Board, signed by me, of the Serbian Democratic Party, and what it says in the second sentence is that the Serbs are fleeing again leaving their ancient thresholds, the thresholds of their forefathers and fathers and have become homeless people without a roof over their heads, without a homeland and without the necessary conditions for life having been respected citizens, and Croatian democracy forced them to do that. And then a little lower down, the Main Board was decided to approach in an organised fashion the collection of assistance in the form of money, food, medicines, clothing, sheets, household equipments, and so on, according to list supplied. Now, may we go on to the last page -- or, rather, the second page. The specifications are set out underwear, clothing for children, men and women, women's clothing, men's clothing, children's clothing, sheets, pillow cases, duvets, blankets and so on, footwear for men and women and children, plates, pots and so on, household goods. Now, do you know where these refugees were from, where they came from, to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we were doing our best to make their life easier? Do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you moved to page 2 before completing page 1. I wonder if I could have a look at the rest of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The part of our people from Croatia are on the move, fleeing, and they're in Vojvodina and Bosnia. Do you want me to read it all out, or are you going to read it out yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute, I'll read it. That's fine. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "Part of our people from Croatia are in flight." Do you know that we had refugees from Croatia in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm aware that there were small numbers of refugees, Serbs from Croatia who had entered Bosnia at that time and were to be found in, as I understand it, Eastern Herzegovina, the Banja Luka and Bosnian Krajina area, and a couple of other areas that are sort of convenient to the conflict that was developing in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what to your mind is a small number of refugees in peacetime in a country that's not at war? What would you call a small number?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the numbers were. I -- some of the documents I've looked at talk about a few tens of people. Others it looks like there are some hundreds. So the numbers did, in fact, grow once conflict became more acute in Croatia in the early fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you really think that we would have to collect aid for dozens of people or hundreds of people? Mr. Donia, we were dealing here with thousands and thousands of refugees. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow we'll be dealing with this question of regionalisation in greater detail, but let's try and recapitulate to see where we stand, how far we've come. Do you agree that up until the 30th of January, 1991, both the SDA and the SDS were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you also agree that the SDS, only on the 30th of January, made public that it would move to adopt documents on independence -- or, rather, sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's a big difference between independence and sovereignty. That's, to my recollection, about the date that the SDS indicated its intention to move for the Assembly to adopt the declaration that we spoke of last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that from that time on there were accelerated efforts, there was this accelerated chain of events which led to tensions rising? There was the attempt to adopt that declaration on sovereignty and its rejection -- or, rather, postponement, and when it was forwarded to the Council for National Equality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it that way. I think the effort to pass the resolution in February, which failed, set off a long period in which the -- that is long and let's say in the next six, seven months, in which the SDA, although it was -- fully intended to resubmit the proposal, basically worked toward arranging an agreement whereby Yugoslavia would be preserved with Bosnia-Herzegovina as having an equal status with all the other republics vis-a-vis Yugoslavia itself. There were certainly things that were going on at that contributed to growing tensions. Most significantly in my mind the rising effort to create separate regional organisations on behalf of the SDS which can be dated from the 21st of January, 1991, and came into full public view in -- in April of 1991. And there were other things that were contributing to the rising tensions, and sometimes tensions rose and sometimes they fell briefly, but as a general proposition, I don't know that the sovereignty declaration played much of a role in those because it was something that had been tried and not -- not passed and then subsequently put in, at least on the back-burner, by the SDA and other issues came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was it that led to the rising tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- there are a number of causes. One was the growing concern among many Bosnians about the behaviour of the Yugoslav People's Army both in prosecuting the campaign on behalf of Serb separatists in Croatia and in its various undertakings in Bosnian starting in the late spring, summer of 1991, which came again into view and were seen by many as the JNA becoming a force supporting Serb rebels in Croatia and allied with the SDS in -- in Bosnia. The various efforts of the parties to acquire arms, yours and that of the SDA, certainly contributed to tensions, as did the growing role of military forces that actually crossed the border from Croatia. Both Croatian forces and the JNA did damage in Bosnia. I guess, to me, one of the factors was the dispatch of the Uzice Corps, which took place in September 1991, sort of a -- viewed by -- or disclaimed by some senior officers of the JNA but was nonetheless was a part of it. So I think there's a lot of causes, and the political forces were at times in contention and at times working together to try to resolve things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, why would the question of the Yugoslav People's Army be a cause of concern? Are you trying to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean in order for it to be living in peace, you're trying to say that everything would be fine if it weren't for the Yugoslav People's Army; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. As I indicated, I think there were a lot of causes, many episodes and some general trends that led to the tensions rising, particularly in the fall of -- late summer, fall of 1991. The behaviour of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, was a cause of concern, and as you recognise from the very beginning when you did not pursue the ministries of interior or defence, the JNA was the most powerful military force in the region. It was one of the most powerful militaries in Europe, and its role, even as it was protesting its impartiality in an attempt to defend Yugoslavia came under question because of its activities particularly in Croatia in the spring of 1991 onward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. With that question and answer, we'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [French and English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing French translation. Let's continue. I think it has been resolved. I think it has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, now I'm going to try to put questions that are going to be as short as possible so that I would get yes or no answers. My position is that the one and only first and foremost reason for tensions is the change in position by Mr. Izetbegovic and the SDA. Instead of being in favour of preserving Yugoslavia, they opted for leaving Yugoslavia on the 30th of January, 1991. That's when the process started. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately you've injected a couple of questions into this one to make it a more complex one, but I reject your position that the only first and foremost reason for tension was the change in position by Mr. Izetbegovic and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not disputing the fact that there were new complications. However, my position is that is the foremost reason. Up until the 30th of January, we had no reason to have tensions. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Mr. Izetbegovic also became president of the Council for the Defence of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that he became that on the 30th of January if that is what your question is meant to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. No. He became president of the Council for the Defence of Muslims. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important to get a date established here. The -- I have recorded that the Council for the Defence of Muslims was founded by the SDA on June 10th, and at that time, it is my understanding that, yes, he did become president of that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our information says that the decision was taken in February, but let it be the way you put it. Do you think that that goes hand-in-hand with his position as president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Yes or no? Is that right? Is it proper for him to be president for the defence of just one ethnic group in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Serbs had certain priorities that were -- well, that had a certain hierarchy amongst themselves and that their first and utmost priority was preserving Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the position as you stated it back in -- in February, namely that if Yugoslavia continued in existence your loyalty would be to Mr. Izetbegovic, and if Yugoslavia disintegrated your loyalty would be to Mr. Milosevic pretty well summed up that position, and I think you adhered to it consistently into -- well into late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that among the Serbs, due to the pressure exerted by developments as they were, there was a change in this hierarchy of priorities, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There did come a time when that change of priorities took place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that all the time while there was a possibility for preserving any kind of Yugoslavia we advocated an all-embracing single Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you were engaged in separatist activities long before the possibility of a -- of preserving Yugoslavia ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When, Mr. Donia, and through which activities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you formed various communities of municipalities which -- which had a separatist political intent in the early months of 1991, you created Serb autonomous regions in the fall of 1991, and in the meantime were engaged in relations with military forces that were embracing separatism as well. So I think that you were very, in many times, ostentatiously supporting separatism long before that possibility of Yugoslavia be -- any kind of Yugoslavia ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that it was Serbs who were separatists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it that the Serbs wanted to separate themselves from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've been talking about in the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and my answer is that Serbs wanted to separate themselves from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They started that movement, as I say -- one can date it to January of 1991 and see it continuing right up until the beginning of war and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, all of that is upsidedown, topsy-turvy, totally wrong. Are you trying to say that we conceived of municipalities not on an economic basis but, rather, for separatist reasons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly am, and I think the history of the formation of the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities is a good illustration of that. When that community was proclaimed on April 25th, 1991, you invited participants from a number of political parties, and including other national parties and members of the opposition, on the premise that that community was going to involve economic development. When those people got to the meeting, they discovered, according to their own accounts, that they were in the midst of a lot of Serbian propaganda. They were offended by the fact that this was a single party undertaking, and, in fact, one of them, Mr. Dodik, who is the present prime minister of Republika Srpska, said he found it the height of political illiteracy and impudence to have this body created by a single political party and said it demanded referral to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I can further show you, in fact, I'd like to, that both the first president of the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities and yourself viewed it as a separatist design. If one goes to paragraph 183 of my excerpts report, one can see that this -- and I'd like to do that if Your Honours would indulge me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure if your report has para numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just for context, Dr. Karadzic, this -- these words were spoken during the 17th session, which was July of 1992, at a time when the municipal strategy of the SDS was going -- undergoing a complete about face, and the party -- you and other party leaders discovered that the municipal associations which had served so well to weaken the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina were now turning out to be weakening the new Serb state and therefore had to be diminished in power, and eventually the regions dissolved. And Mr. Vojo Kupresanin was the person who had been elected the president of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina on the 25th of April, 1992. And at that time, he gave an address -- address in which he stressed that the purpose of the association was to express solidarity with the Serbs of Croatia and contribute to the economic self-sufficiency of Krajina. And what he said was, speaking of 1991: "Last year we built up the region and made it strong with a clear purpose and goal. The task of the region of Krajina was to destroy Alija's state. I think that other regions followed suit, and we were successful in that respect. If we continue to affirm the region, we will undermine the Serbian state," meaning the Bosnian Serb state. "We mustn't do that. We will now find possibilities and ways to affirm this state and make it efficient. We are becoming aware of what decentralisation can do to a state in which we have invested considerable live, casualties and efforts. I think we should opt for maximum centralisation not only because of the war but also because we are a newly formed state. Wan see that only very centralised states in the world are, in fact, successful, effective and achieve best results." And, in fact, you express very similar sentiments -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, sir, that we go back to what it was that I was trying to say. You have already moved on to the war and the period after the war. I asked you first and foremost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue your question, can I know where it is in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it's item number 179. It's on page 71, it -- title's at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's e-court page 75 of the document. The hard copy page, as Dr. Donia said, 73, but e-court page 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thematic excerpts. I was looking at the wrong one. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, let's not skip anything. Let's not skip periods of time or actual events. Is it not correct that from the very outset our only demand was to change the community of municipalities and that the SDA had accepted that and they went into a coalition with us without any objections in that regard? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They objected strenuously when you proclaimed the community of municipalities, because it was so clearly the creation of a single party on behalf of a single people and without any inclination to pursue the economic development goals that you had cited in the invitation for people to come to this meeting on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not correct. We're going to deal with that tomorrow. I'm asking you about our pre-election programme. Did we ask for anything else but for reorganisation of the community of municipalities? Is that when we announced SAOs and regionalisation, or was that only at the level of the community of municipalities? Yes or no? Let's do it this way. You're not in charge of this cross-examination. Just answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Karadzic, just a minute. When you ask a question in cross-examination, you get the answer which the witness considers to be appropriate unless he is stopped by the Tribunal. You can not control the answer. You can only control the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I'm asking for nothing to be skipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm talking about the pre-election period. In relation to the territorial organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what did we ask for? Was it not that we only asked for a reorganisation of the community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked for many things, of course, in the course of the electoral campaign. Some of them related to this theme and many not. You asked for a reorganisation or a redrawing of municipal boundaries, and you asked for a reconstruction of the communities of municipalities that then existed and advocated moving as you indicated in your questioning, advocating moving the centres of those, seats of those communities of municipalities to smaller towns or towns which had a much larger Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that we started mentioning the SAOs and establishing the SAOs only towards the end of May or the beginning of June, after everything else had happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina politically?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, you established the SAOs only in September and October. You established the communities of municipalities in this period of late April, May, and June. You established the Bosnian Krajina one, as I indicated, on the 26th of April -- I'm sorry, 25th of April, in Banja Luka and kept the seat of the former community of municipalities in Banja Luka. So there was no change in the seat of the community of municipalities as you had proposed earlier. This process then went on for the next several weeks in which you proclaimed the community of municipalities of Herzegovina and also Romanija and a few other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the community of municipalities of Krajina invited the Muslim municipalities to join them as well, because they had had enough of Sarajevo and they wanted to develop better from an economic point of view and to become more economically independent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the COBK community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina invited all municipalities in the area to join. No municipalities joined other than those with an absolute Serb majority or near an absolute majority simply because both the opposition -- or the opposition national parties and the left opposition became convinced that this had nothing to do with economic development. It was simply a power grab by the SDS and that's why they turned that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it that was in power in these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in, I think, all cases the municipalities that declined to join were either governed by the -- or the SDA or by a coalition of the SDA and HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Municipalities that had joined in had the SDS in power anyway; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, had the SDS -- oh, okay. I misunderstood your questions. The municipalities that joined all had the SDS in power, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the SDS did not need to grab power. They were in power already; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seized power at the level of the community of municipalities, and, in fact, as their programme unfolded what they did was to take over the existing economic resources of the former community of municipalities in the name of the Serb people and so acquired them rather than take -- doing anything that developed new wealth and new economic initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll look at that eventually. So the Serb objective was to preserve Yugoslavia. Do you agree that the Serbs considered Yugoslavia to be their home? When they said that they had built a home in 1918, do you believe that the Serbs considered Yugoslavia to be their home?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think virtually all Serbs did. Many Serbs came to believe, or some Serbs anyway, came to belive that the Yugoslavia that they called their home had changed dramatically in character in the period of the Milosevic governance, but, nevertheless, I think that the vast majority of Serbs did, in fact, feel that Yugoslavia was their home, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that after that first and uppermost objective the second objective in terms of this hierarchy was, among the Serbs, that is, that if the Croats and Slovenes were leaving Yugoslavia the Serbs should remain within Yugoslavia in those territories that were predominantly Serb and that Bosnia should remain in Yugoslavia if at all possible. So was that not our second priority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Greater Serbia essentially is what -- what you are suggesting; is that right? Your second priority was a Greater Serbia. Or am I misrepresenting what your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not a Greater Serbia. It is a Yugoslavia as big as possible. Did you not find that in all our public speeches? How could that be a greater -- Greater Serbia if it were to include Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia? I mean, even if Croatia were to leave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- the programme that you embraced and that Mr. Milosevic embraced also included holding on to those parts of Croatia which Serbs claimed as their land, and thus it wasn't completely congruent with the remaining republics as they were then bounded by -- by the boundaries of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: None of that's how it was and we'll clear that up, but did those Serbs want to remain in Yugoslavia? Not Milosevic, the Serbs living in Krajina or Bosnia. Did they wish to stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of them did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was Yugoslavia a sovereign and the sole recognised state amongst all those entities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until January 15th, yes. January 15th, 1992, that was the status, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How then could the Serbs have been separatists if they were calling to remain in the country that they saw as their home, a home which was internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were seeking to separate from Bosnia-Herzegovina and undertook all kinds of initiatives and activities to so separate, and, in fact, one delegate at the 3rd Bosnian Assembly session in December 1991 asked exactly the question that arises from this. He said: "If we are to stay in Yugoslavia, why do we have to take all these actions to separate from Bosnia? Why can't we just let them separate from us?" But that was not the situation. The situation was that you were taking various initiatives to separate from Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as to inhibit the work of its government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would that have been the case if Bosnia-Herzegovina had not undertaken secessionist steps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I really don't want to speculate on what might have happened if something else had happened. I would only point out that the effort to form the community of municipalities dates from January 21, which is long before this whole issue of secessionism on the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its proclamations of sovereignty arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, and just yes or no, please, is what you're saying this: That the Serbs would have separated from Bosnia even if Bosnia had remained in Yugoslavia? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just -- that's a speculative -- that would be sure speculation. I, you know, really can't -- can't say that. I don't have that much insight into what Serb intentions would have been in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that the third in the hierarchy, third position in the hierarchy of Serb interests and aspirations was to create in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if it were to step down from Yugoslavia, their own constituent unit and that that unit should be independent? What was called the Republika Srpska, to create Republika Srpska and for Republika Srpska to be independent.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the fourth point, a painful one, the fourth compromise as we called it, for the whole of Bosnia to step down from Yugoslavia and to remain integral and that that Serbian constituent unit should remain in Bosnia without being independent.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't -- I don't see a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is this: The fourth painful compromise, as we referred to it, was that that Serbian constituent unit should not be independent of Bosnia, just autonomous within Bosnia and to have the Serbs accept the boundaries, external boundaries, of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I don't see a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
